planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants after the last frost in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in shade to partial shade; established colonies self-sow freely by spores in Gulf Coast gardens, so site it where volunteer seedlings are welcome.

directions: This fast-growing Asian and Pacific Island fern has naturalized throughout the Deep South and Gulf Coast, forming loose clumps of soft, yellow-green fronds that are two to three times pinnately divided into a broad, lacy triangle. New fiddleheads unfurl covered in reddish-brown hairs, adding seasonal interest before expanding into arching three- to four-foot fronds. It thrives in the deep, damp shade under live oaks and pines where few other ferns will grow vigorously, and dies back to the crown after a hard freeze before flushing again in spring. Because it self-sows readily from spores, gardeners in warm zones often let it colonize naturalized woodland beds rather than confining it to a formal border.

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; give the slowly spreading rhizome room to form a dense evergreen clump over several seasons before dividing.

directions: Native to woodlands of China, Japan, and Taiwan, this holly fern produces broadly triangular, leathery fronds divided into glossy, spine-toothed pinnae that hold their deep green color through winter in mild climates. The widely grown selection sold as 'Variegata' carries a bright chartreuse-yellow stripe down the center of each frond, giving it a variegated, almost tropical look in a plant hardy well into the mid-Atlantic and lower Midwest. It forms a tidy, slowly spreading clump rather than running aggressively, making it a good structural anchor fern for a shaded border or woodland path edge. Unlike many holly ferns it tolerates a bit more winter cold and a bit more garden moisture than Cyrtomium falcatum.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions after all danger of frost in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the creeping rhizome spreads to knit together a dense groundcover under palms and tree canopies in frost-free gardens.

directions: Palapalai is a soft-textured, rhizomatous fern native to Hawaii and tropical Asia-Pacific forests, prized in Hawaiian culture for its fragrance and its traditional use in lei and hula adornment. Its finely cut, bright yellow-green fronds emerge in loose, overlapping ranks from a creeping rhizome, quickly filling in as an informal groundcover beneath palms, bananas, and other broad-leaved tropical shade plants. It prefers filtered light rather than deep shade and needs steady moisture and humidity to keep its delicate fronds from browning at the tips. In frost-free zone 9b-11 gardens it stays evergreen and spreads readily; farther north it is best grown as a container or greenhouse specimen.
sources: University of Hawaii at Manoa CTAHR Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Plant in sharply drained, sandy soil in partial shade to light dappled sun, mimicking the open pine flatwoods and coastal uplands where it grows wild; established plants tolerate considerable drought and need little supplemental water once rooted in.

directions: A Florida and Caribbean native found in dry pine flatwoods, scrub margins, and coastal hammocks, pine fern forms a low clump of wiry, near-black stipes topped with twice-pinnate, deltoid fronds that resemble a coarse maidenhair fern. Its fertile fronds are distinctive within the fern world: rather than bearing spores on the leaf undersides, they produce narrow, upright fertile pinnae held above the sterile foliage, a hallmark of the flowering-fern family Anemiaceae. Unlike most shade ferns it is genuinely drought tolerant once established, making it a useful textural accent for dry, sandy shade under pines where moisture-loving ferns struggle. It stays evergreen in the warmest parts of its range and dies back after hard freezes in zone 8b.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants, University of South Florida
